claim: 33% of people aged 16-74 in the EU had used generative AI tools in the previous three months
exact_source_location: Eurostat Statistics Explained, "Use of artificial intelligence by individuals", section "Who uses generative AI?" (oldid 705051; data extracted March 2026)
population: Individuals aged 16-74 in EU survey scope
reference_period: 2025 wave; previous three months; fieldwork generally Q2 asking about Q1
gender_measure: Source sex categories Male/Female only (questionnaire item H2)
limits: No published standard error in the inspected article or table; single wave so no trend; EU aggregate is not a world figure
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Country spread is wide in the same table: Denmark 48%, Romania 18%

claim: In the EU in 2025 men used generative AI slightly more than women, 35% versus 30%
exact_source_location: Eurostat Statistics Explained, same article, section "Who uses generative AI?"
population: Individuals aged 16-74 in EU survey scope
limits: 5.0 pp absolute; roughly 14% of men's rate. Eurostat itself states gender "is less of a predictor" than age or education. No published uncertainty; no sex-by-occupation crossing exists in this table
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Same article: age 16-24 64% versus 65-74 7%; high education 49% versus low 22% - both far larger than the sex difference

claim: UK adults: 63.2% of male and 55.5% of female respondents reported using AI in the previous three months
exact_source_location: DSIT Public Engagement Survey 2025/2026, artificial intelligence workbook Table_E5 rows 38-39, columns B-F
unit_and_denominator: people; weighted estimates on unweighted bases 13,902 male and 15,953 female
gender_measure: Provider categories from questionnaire item GENDER, four published categories
design: Address-based stratified random sample; web/paper; descriptive
verification_status: verified by coordinator extract (dsit-published-cells.json), not re-derived here
limits: Use definition includes autonomous workplace AI (Notes!B16), so not equivalent to the Eurostat measure; UK covers ages above 74; no confidence interval in the inspected cells
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Same table publishes "identify in another way" 49.2% (base 99) and "prefer not to say" 45.0% (base 671); both need visible precision caveats

claim: US adults: 50% of men and 47% of women say they ever use AI chatbots, against 39% and 28% in 2024
exact_source_location: Pew Research Center, "The gender gap in AI", chart "Men, women are now equally likely to say they use chatbots" data table
verification_status: verified: chapter and chart data tables read 2026-10-01
limits: 2024 item wording differed and was asked only of those who had heard at least a little about chatbots, so the 2024-2026 change is not a clean trend; "ever use" is not current use
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The same report shows a persisting gap in daily use (27% of men, 20% of women), so "the gap has closed" is outcome-specific

claim: Brazil: among internet users, 35% of male and 30% of female respondents used generative AI tools
exact_source_location: Cetic.br TIC Domicilios 2025, individuals table M1, SEXO rows (total 32% yes)
population: Internet users aged 10 and over in Brazil
reference_period: 2025 survey; reference window not stated on the table page
limits: Denominator is internet users, not all individuals, and age starts at 10; reference period, sampling and precision not established here; site licence shown as CC BY-SA 4.0 but table-level reuse terms need the steward's audit
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The 35/30 split is numerically identical to the EU figures in P02 on a different denominator and age range - an illustration of why these cannot be pooled

claim: Canada: rounded workplace generative-AI use was 22% for women and 22% for men, while the adjusted odds ratio for Male+ versus Female+ was 1.15 (95% CI 1.02-1.29)
exact_source_location: Statistics Canada, Canadian Survey on Business Conditions-linked worker article 75-006-X 2026001 00007, Table A.1
reference_period: Four collection periods, September 2024 - July 2025; use in the main job in the past 12 months
gender_measure: Male+ / Female+ after confidentiality aggregation of nonbinary respondents
verification_status: verified by coordinator within this assignment; the source URL is blocked to this session's fetch tool
limits: Crude parity and an adjusted male-favouring association are different quantities; the odds ratio must not be restated as a percentage-point gap or a causal effect; territories excluded
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: This is the clearest single case in the register where the unconditional and the adjusted comparison point in different directions

claim: Pooling 54 source-outcome entries covering 318,924 respondents or observed users gives sample-size-weighted adoption of 47.8% for men and 39.3% for women, an 8.5 pp absolute and 21.7% relative gap
exact_source_location: Cranney, Delecourt and Koning, HBS Working Paper 25-023, May 2026, section 4.1 p.8 and footnote 5
population: 58 plotted sources spanning more than one hundred countries; sampling frames from national panels to single-firm traces
gender_measure: Self-reported gender in most sources; name-inferred in some
limits: The authors pool across "ever use", weekly use, workplace use and tool-specific use, so this is a weighted average of incompatible measures and not a population rate for any defined population; it must not be presented as a world rate; the authors themselves flag publication and reporting bias (Appendix A)
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The paper's own 2025-2026 restriction gives 39.8% and 34.4% across 16 entries, N=113,981: 5.4 pp and 15.7% (footnote 1 p.3)

claim: The raw gender gap is positive in 56 of 58 plotted sources and negative in 2, ranging from 23.6 pp favouring men to 3.0 pp favouring women
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, p.8 and pp.9-10
limits: Direction consistency across publications is not statistical independence; several entries draw on the same survey programmes, and 18 further corpus sources could not be plotted at all
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Named female-advantage cases: BCG tech employees (+3%, driven by senior technical roles), Spanish journalism students (94.48% female versus 91.53% male), UAE students (Shishakly)

claim: Men report more frequent chatbot use than women in the US: 27% versus 20% use them daily
exact_source_location: Pew, "The gender gap in AI", bullet "But a higher share of men use these tools regularly"
limits: Self-reported frequency; no published interval in the inspected page
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Coexists with parity on ever-use (P04), so participation and intensity must be reported separately

claim: US tool mix differs by gender while ChatGPT does not: Gemini 29% versus 20%, Copilot 22% versus 13%, Grok 11% versus 4%, Claude 9% versus 4%, ChatGPT 44% versus 44%, Meta AI 13% versus 15%
exact_source_location: Pew, same chapter, chart "Men are more likely than women to report using Gemini, Copilot and Grok" data table
limits: Differences are computed from rounded values; Pew marks only some as statistically significant; Meta AI is the one female-higher entry and is not flagged significant
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: A single headline adoption indicator would hide this; tool-level composition is where the US gap now sits

claim: Across the ten most visited US AI tools the female share of visits ranges from 44.1% on chatgpt.com to 26.7% on grok.com
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, Table 1 p.37
population: Visits to ten highest-traffic consumer AI domains in the US
unit_and_denominator: visits, not people; share of panel traffic
limits: Visits are not people; vendor demographic imputation is undocumented here; excludes app and logged-out use; cannot be compared with survey adoption rates
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The same table shows women's mean visits are longer on character.ai (+9.8%) and polybuzz.ai (+11.6%) - female-higher intensity in companion-oriented products

claim: Worldwide, the female share of traffic to the ten highest-traffic AI tools rose from just under 35% in January 2023 to about 40% in January 2026 and has been broadly flat since October 2024
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, section 4.2 p.11 and Figure 3 p.34
population: Visits to ten highest-traffic consumer AI domains worldwide
limits: The plotted band is a cross-domain interval, not a sampling interval for a population; country-level cells for smaller countries are noisy on the authors' own account
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Not a measure of how many women use AI; a stable traffic share is consistent with several different changes in the underlying user base

claim: Women are slightly more likely than men to say they use chatbots for emotional support or advice (11% versus 8%), with no difference for companionship (4% versus 4%)
exact_source_location: Pew, same chapter, chart "Men are more likely than women to say they use chatbots for search, work" data table
limits: Small differences on rounded values; purposes are multiple-response
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Men lead on search (45/39), work tasks among employed adults (40/35), fun (28/22) and news (15/12)

claim: In the EU, private use is the most common purpose; over 50% of generative-AI users aged 25-64 report work-related purposes and 62% of users aged 16-24 report formal education purposes
exact_source_location: Eurostat Statistics Explained, same article, section "What do people use generative AI for?" and Figure 2
population: Individuals aged 16-74 who used generative AI in the previous three months
gender_measure: Not applicable: this figure is broken down by age, not sex
limits: This published article presents purposes by age only. A sex-by-purpose breakdown is not shown here and must not be inferred from it; purposes are multiple-response so they do not sum to 100
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The index's purpose row (EU_PURPOSE) depends on denominators that the steward has flagged; work-purpose denominators are not restricted to workers

claim: The most common single main reason EU non-users give is that they do not feel the need (64%), followed by not being sure how to use the tools (14%), not being aware of them (9%) and privacy or security concerns (7%)
exact_source_location: Eurostat Statistics Explained, same article, section "What is stopping people from using AI?" and Figure 3
population: Recent internet users in the EU who had not used generative AI in the previous three months
gender_measure: Not shown by sex in this article
limits: Single-response item, so these are mutually exclusive main reasons and not a full account of barriers; reported reasons are not causal explanations of the adoption gap; this article does not split them by sex
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Same sample family as P01-P02 and EU_NONUSE; never count as independent evidence

claim: US men are more likely than women to say they have heard a lot about AI (55% versus 41%) and to be extremely or very confident using chatbots (22% versus 15%)
exact_source_location: Pew, same chapter, chart "Men are more likely than women to say they've heard a lot about AI, chatbots" and section "Confidence in using chatbots"
limits: Self-assessed familiarity and confidence are not objective knowledge or skill
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Familiarity and confidence gaps persist in the same survey in which the ever-use gap has closed

claim: US men are more likely than women to say chatbots help their productivity (35% versus 25%), with modest or no differences for knowledge, creativity, happiness or relationships
exact_source_location: Pew, same chapter, chart "Men are more likely than women to say chatbots help their productivity" data table
limits: Perceived helpfulness is a belief, not a measured productivity outcome; the item is asked of all adults, not only users
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Humlum and Vestergaard reportedly find no average gender gap in expected time savings but greater uncertainty among women (reported in Cranney et al. p.18; not verified at source here)

claim: Women in the US are more negative about AI's future than men: 43% versus 36% expect a negative societal impact and 68% versus 58% say AI is advancing too quickly
exact_source_location: Pew, same chapter, charts "Women are more negative about the future of AI than men" and "Women are more likely to think AI is advancing too quickly" data tables
limits: Attitudes are not adoption; direction of any relationship is not established by this survey
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Stephany and Duszynski argue the association runs through societal risk perception (B05); a Pew cross-section cannot separate cause from rationalisation

claim: In UK tracker data, the gender gap in frequent personal generative-AI use is largest among younger, digitally fluent respondents with high societal-risk concerns, exceeding 45 percentage points in that subgroup
exact_source_location: Stephany and Duszynski, arXiv:2601.03880v2 (submitted 7 January 2026, revised 30 July 2026), abstract
population: Nationally representative UK adults, Public Attitudes to Data and AI Tracker
gender_measure: Tracker gender categories (binary in the reported analysis)
design: Descriptive, random-forest prediction and score-matched comparison of repeated cross-sections
verification_status: abstract verified 2026-10-01; full text not read in this session
limits: An intersectional subgroup figure, not an average gap; score matching on repeated cross-sections is associational, not causal; the authors' own framing is a "behavioural pathway", not an identified effect
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Eurostat's non-user data (B01) place privacy and security concerns at only 7% of main reasons, so risk concern is a strong predictor in one design and a minor stated reason in another

claim: Across 35 European countries, workplace generative-AI adoption ranges from under 3% to 25%; occupational exposure strongly predicts uptake, a gender gap persists and is concentrated in the most exposed occupations, and a shift-share design finds no detectable effect of adoption on worker-reported task restructuring
exact_source_location: Henseke, "From Exposure to Adoption: Generative AI in European Workplaces", arXiv:2604.18849v3 (28 April 2026), abstract
design: Cross-sectional gradients plus a shift-share design
verification_status: abstract verified 2026-10-01; full text not read; the register's assignment of this record to the EWCS_2024 sample family is NOT confirmed by the abstract
limits: No gap magnitude is given in the abstract; "no detectable effect" is not evidence of no effect and the abstract itself reads it as an early integration phase; the underlying survey must be confirmed before this is used as a workplace indicator
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: If the source is EWCS 2024, it shares a sample family with the EWCS_WORK indicator row and must not be counted as separate evidence

claim: Among a register-linked sample of 17,907 Danish workers in 11 AI-exposed occupations, women were about 16 percentage points less likely than men in the same occupation to have used ChatGPT for work
exact_source_location: Reported in Cranney et al., WP 25-023, p.12, citing Humlum and Vestergaard (2025), PNAS 122(1):e2414972121
population: Danish workers in 11 specified AI-exposed occupations; representative within those occupations
unit_and_denominator: people; workers who had heard of ChatGPT (work-purpose item Q7)
design: Survey linked to administrative registers; descriptive within occupation
verification_status: UNVERIFIED at source: the DOI was not accessible from this session; all detail here is secondary from Cranney et al.
limits: Secondary reporting of a magnitude; the outcome is derived from a purpose question among those who had used ChatGPT, so the denominator needs checking at source; 11 occupations in one country are not a national workforce
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Widely repeated claims that employer encouragement cuts the gap to 5 pp and training to 3.6 pp appear in the project's historical landscape note and were NOT verified in this session

claim: In an EU-wide working-age survey, gender was not a significant factor explaining AI use at work once occupation, education, age, firm size, nationality, income, tenure and country were controlled
exact_source_location: Reported in Cranney et al., WP 25-023, Table A3 p.57, describing Gonzalez Vazquez et al. (2025), AIM-WORK, full sample N = 70,316 and regression sample N = 42,433
population: Working-age population across all 27 EU Member States
verification_status: UNVERIFIED at source: taken from Cranney et al.'s one-line summary; the JRC report was not read in this session
limits: A non-significant coefficient does not establish absence of a difference, and controlling for occupation answers a different question from the unconditional gap
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Directly in tension with Cranney et al.'s headline that the gap is "not reducible to occupational segregation" (p.9); the two use different estimands

claim: Frontier tool use shows a much wider relative gap than general use in the same sample: 22% of respondents with typically male names versus 9% with typically female names reported using coding agents more than once a week, against 81% versus 78% for any research use of generative AI
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, p.12 and footnote 9 p.12, reporting Lyttelton, Massenkoff and Wilmers (2026)
population: Active quantitative social scientists recruited by email; name-classified subgroup n = 561 typically male and 374 typically female (full survey N = 1,260)
verification_status: verified as reported in Cranney et al. 2026-10-01; the underlying Anthropic report was not read in this session
limits: Name-inferred gender is a proxy and is not respondent identity; a recruited disciplinary sample is not a workforce; the 144% relative figure is a ratio of two small shares
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The same sample shows near-parity on broad adoption, so the frontier-versus-general distinction matters more than the headline adoption gap here

claim: Female-dominated occupations are almost twice as likely to be exposed to generative AI as male-dominated ones: 29% versus 16%, with mixed occupations at 28%
exact_source_location: ILO Research Brief, "Gen AI, occupational segregation and gender equality in the world of work", March 2026, key points p.1 and Figure 5 p.6
population: 436 ISCO-08 4-digit occupations with reliable data (82 female-dominated, 89 male-dominated, 266 mixed), applied to employment in 84 countries
reference_period: Latest year available per country, as early as 2014 for some
unit_and_denominator: occupations, not workers; share of occupations in exposure gradients 1-4
gender_measure: Occupational sex composition thresholds (75%/25%), NOT individual gender
design: Task-based exposure index (ILO-NASK, Gmyrek et al. 2025) applied to harmonised microdata
verification_status: verified: full brief read 2026-10-01; DOI 10.54394/00033798; CC BY 4.0
limits: The unit is occupations, not people, and exposure is modelled potential, not an observed outcome; the brief states explicitly that exposure in gradients 1-4 does not imply near-term redundancy; country reference years differ widely
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The brief's own emphasis is that for most occupations the impact runs through tasks, skills and working conditions rather than job loss (p.1, p.9)

claim: 16% of female-dominated occupations fall in the two highest exposure gradients against 3% of male-dominated ones, and the female-dominated occupations concerned are mainly in the business administration and clerical support cluster
exact_source_location: ILO Research Brief, p.6 and Annex table 1 p.16
limits: Still occupations rather than workers; gradient 4 named examples are typists, accounting and bookkeeping clerks and payroll clerks - occupations already shrinking for other reasons
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Male-dominated occupations in gradients 3-4 are concentrated in ICT (software developers, web developers), which is also where frontier-tool adoption is highest (W04)

claim: Women in employment are more exposed to generative AI than men in 88% of the countries in the sample, with the highest female exposure (over 40% of female employment) in Pacific and Caribbean small island states, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and the Philippines
exact_source_location: ILO Research Brief, p.6 and Figure 6 p.7
population: Employment by occupation and sex in 84 countries with reliable 4-digit ISCO data
reference_period: Latest year available per country (printed in Figure 6)
unit_and_denominator: employment shares; share of female and male employment in gradients 1-4
gender_measure: Occupational sex composition applied to employment
limits: Country reference years are not aligned, so this is not a synchronous cross-country comparison; countries where women are less exposed are mainly high-agriculture or low female participation settings, which is a composition effect rather than protection
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: 41% of employment is exposed in high-income countries against 11% in low-income countries (p.6), so exposure tracks economic structure at least as much as gender

claim: High AI exposure in a job may be as likely to be good news as bad, because the most AI-exposed UK occupational groups tend to have more work activities and higher typical qualifications, which makes augmentation more likely than automation
exact_source_location: Tera Allas, "AI and jobs: when exposure is a strength", 16 April 2026, sections "AI-exposed jobs are, on average, more complex" and closing paragraphs
reference_period: Chart combines DfE exposure data, O*NET-derived dimensionality and Census 2021 qualification levels
gender_measure: None: this post contains no gender analysis
design: Interpretive essay with descriptive occupational analysis
verification_status: verified: full public post read 2026-10-01; the linked task-bundling working paper is a Dropbox file that was not readable, so the supporting analysis remains unverified
limits: A mechanism argument, not an estimated effect; the UK figures quoted for functional managers and directors (employment +3.5% a year and wages +3.1% a year, 2004-2025) are the author's own calculations with no table reference, and were not reproduced; the author states her Frey-Osborne replication data are not published
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The post's own exception is administrative and secretarial occupations, already in decline - precisely the female-dominated gradient 3-4 cluster in E02. Allas and the OpenAI framework she links are one interpretive lineage, not independent confirmation

claim: Women made up about 30% of the AI workforce in 2022 and under 10% of engineers and software developers
exact_source_location: ILO Research Brief, p.10, citing WEF (2023) and ILOSTAT (2023)
verification_status: the brief statement was read 2026-10-01; the underlying WEF and ILOSTAT series were NOT checked
limits: A compiled secondary figure with definitional variation across sources; the brief also cites a LinkedIn-based 29.2% figure for STEM workers, a different construct on proprietary data
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: Representation in building AI is a different construct from using it and should not be mixed into a participation indicator

claim: A persistent 16% usage gap could result in hundreds of billions of dollars of lost productivity and growth in the US alone
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, conclusion p.19, resting on Baily, Brynjolfsson and Korinek (2023)
limits: This is an extrapolation that multiplies an aggregate productivity-potential figure by a usage gap; it assumes use causes the gains, that the gap would persist, and that women's forgone use maps proportionally onto output. It is not an estimated economic cost and should not be reported as one
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: The same paper's conclusion notes the opposite possibility - that lower adoption could benefit women if AI erodes skills or learning - and cites evidence of AI raising the quantity but reducing the quality of academic writing

claim: The Global Index on Responsible AI 2026 (second edition) scores 135 countries and jurisdictions on 38 indicators across five dimensions, drawing on 1,872 reviewed documents
exact_source_location: global-index.ai landing page, sections "Key Findings", "Evidence Explorer" and the comparison table
gender_measure: Gender enters as governance indicators (Gender Equality policy; Gender Gap in Mobile Internet), not as user gender
verification_status: verified: landing page read 2026-10-01; methodology page not read
limits: Measures government policy and governance conditions, not people's use, experience or outcomes; policy scores must never be read as user outcomes
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: It does publish gender findings - 29 new countries addressing gender and AI since the first edition, and only 24 of 55 countries with gender frameworks showing implementation evidence - so the differentiation claim must be about construct, not about "nobody covers gender"

claim: GIRAI's 2026 key findings state that 53% of the global population has used generative AI tools
exact_source_location: global-index.ai landing page, key finding 01 "Governance"
verification_status: the statement was read 2026-10-01; its source and method are NOT identified on the page and were not traced
limits: No population denominator, reference period, survey basis or uncertainty is given on the page. This figure must not be reused, and it is a concrete example of the pooled world rate that landscape v1 declines to produce
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: No verified source in this register supports a single worldwide generative-AI use rate for men or for women

claim: Near parity among ChatGPT consumer accounts by mid-2025 and a 44.1% female share of US chatgpt.com visits over the same period are both reported, and reflect different populations rather than a contradiction
exact_source_location: Cranney et al., WP 25-023, pp.13-14 and footnotes 10-11, discussing Chatterji et al. (2025)
population: Eligible logged-in ChatGPT consumer-plan accounts active in a week, versus all website visits
gender_measure: Both name-inferred or vendor-imputed, with a 20-30% unknown-gender category in the provider study
verification_status: verified as reported in Cranney et al. 2026-10-01; Chatterji et al. not read at source here
limits: Neither measure has a population at risk, so neither can produce an adoption rate; excluding unknown-gender accounts raises the estimated female share; business, enterprise, education and logged-out use are outside the provider sample
contrary_or_qualifying_evidence: This pair is the register's clearest demonstration that a parity headline and a gap headline can be simultaneously true on different denominators
